result.note: Tests the September 2026 emergency order on captive coal plants, the causes of the power shortfall, and the depletion of coal stocks.

questions.prompt: In September 2026, India ordered 112 coal-fired captive power plants to maximise generation from October to December and sell surplus electricity to the grid. Consider the following statements in this context:
items: The order covers plants supplying industries such as steel mills and aluminium smelters.
Weaker rainfall reduced hydroelectric generation, forcing coal plants to compensate.
Nighttime electricity shortages in September 2026 were lower than the shortfalls of the preceding summer.
questions.ask: Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.explain: Statement 3 is wrong. Nighttime shortages reached 7.7 gigawatts in September, exceeding the summer shortfalls. Earlier, in March, disrupted gas supplies had prompted preparations to force imported-coal plants to raise generation.
questions.source: Nighttime electricity shortages reached 7.7 gigawatts in September, exceeding this year’s summer shortfalls.

questions.prompt: By late September 2026, power-station coal stocks in India had fallen sharply since the end of August. Roughly how many days' supply did they hold without replenishment?
questions.explain: Coal stocks at power stations fell 24% between end-August and 26 September, leaving roughly seven days' supply. Relief was uneven: cooler weather and extra power purchases helped Kerala avoid cuts on September 24–25.
questions.source: Power-station coal stocks fell 24% between end-August and 26 September, leaving roughly seven days’ supply without replenishment.
